e.etymology: A spelling of Cheryl, a 20th-century English name that probably blends Cherie or Cherry with the ending of Beryl.
A phonetic spelling of Leonard, from the Germanic words for lion and for brave or hardy.
An American coinage of the 1980s that joins the prefix Ka- with the -nesha of Tanesha.
A spelling of Jared, from Hebrew Yered, descent, a forefather of Noah in the Book of Genesis.
The feminine of Elbert, a form of Albert, from Germanic words for noble and bright. The Elberta peach, bred in Georgia in the 1870s, carries the name.
A misspelling of Marguerite, the French form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl. In French marguerite is also the daisy.
From the word Creole, used for the people and culture of French and Spanish colonial Louisiana. It was a girl's name in the South around 1900.
A surname used as a first name. The surname is usually a spelling of Miner, the occupation, and matches Latin minor, smaller or younger.
e.note: Identical to the word minor, meaning lesser or under age.

e.etymology: A spelling of Junius, a Roman family name linked with the goddess Juno. Lucius Junius Brutus was the traditional founder of the Roman Republic.
An elaboration of Cleo, from Greek kleos, glory, with the ending of names like Leora and Flora.
An American coinage of the 1970s that puts the prefix La- before Sonya, the Russian pet form of Sophia.
The Spanish pet form of Concepcion, a name honoring the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary. Concha is also the Spanish word for a seashell.

assoc.t: concha, the shell-topped Mexican sweet bread
concha, vulgar slang for vagina in Argentina and Chile

e.note: Concha is a vulgar slang word in Argentina, Chile and Uruguay; elsewhere it means a shell or a sweet bread.

e.etymology: A spelling of Dustin, an English surname thought to come from the Old Norse name Thorsteinn, Thor's stone.
A blend of Margaret or Marge with Jean, or with the -ene ending, used in the 1920s and 1930s.
A pet form of Jefferson or Jeffrey. Around 1900 it was given to girls as well as boys in the American South.
A Scottish name first recorded in the 1870s, probably from the Hebridean island of Rona, whose Old Norse name means rough island.
e.note: Sounds the same as rona, the 2020 slang for the coronavirus.

e.etymology: A pet form of Temperance, one of the virtue names favored by the Puritans.
A form of Cheryl with the French-style -elle ending. Its mid-1980s rise in the United States followed the R&B singer Cherrelle.
A spelling of Carrie, the pet form of Caroline, a feminine form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man.
namesakes: Carry Nation (temperance crusader who smashed saloons with a hatchet)

e.etymology: Clara with the -ine ending. Clara is the feminine of Latin clarus, clear, bright or famous.
A feminine form of Albert, from the Germanic words adal, noble, and beraht, bright, made with the Latin ending -ina.
A spelling of Iesha, an American form of Aisha, from Arabic for living. The 1991 hit song Iesha by Another Bad Creation set off a burst of the name.
A spelling of Earline, a feminine form of Earl, the English title, from Old English eorl, nobleman.
A spelling of Merle, from French merle, blackbird, which reached English as a surname and nickname. Both men and women carried it.
An English surname from the Old English personal name Maerwine, made of maere, famous, and wine, friend.
Almon is a town in the territory of Benjamin in the Book of Joshua, a name usually read as hidden in Hebrew. It was used as a first name in the 19th-century United States.
A short form of old Germanic names built on aud or od, wealth or fortune. It is a current girl's name in Norway.
namesakes: Oda Mae Brown (the psychic played by Whoopi Goldberg in Ghost)

e.etymology: A spelling of Brittany, the English name of the region in northwest France settled by Britons. It was a leading American girl's name around 1990.
A spelling of Kathy, the short form of Katherine, from the Greek name Aikaterine, long linked with katharos, pure.
